notes.meaning: The woman's husband wonders why she is visiting Elisha on an ordinary day. Pious Israelites often visited prophets on holy days like the New Moon and Sabbath for religious instruction. She shields her husband from the painful truth for now, answering that everything is fine.

She saddles a donkey and tells her servant to ride at full speed without slowing down unless told. Mount Carmel was a journey of fifteen miles or more, so her quick pace showed her urgent need. Her swift actions showed her determination to reach God's prophet without delay.

She arrives at Mount Carmel, where Elisha often stayed and taught. Seeing her from a distance on the mountain, Elisha recognizes her and points her out to his servant Gehazi. Her unexpected, hurried arrival alerts the prophet that something serious must have happened.

Elisha sends Gehazi running to ask whether she, her husband, and her child are well. She brushes off his questions by replying that all is well. She chose to keep her deep sorrow hidden until she could speak to Elisha himself.

When she reaches Elisha on the hill, she falls down and grasps his feet in desperate grief. Gehazi tries to push her away, thinking her action is improper, but Elisha stops him. Elisha explains that her soul is deeply troubled, and the Lord chose not to reveal the reason to him beforehand.

She reminds Elisha that she had never begged for a son or wanted false hopes. Her painful words show that losing the promised boy felt even more heartbreaking than never having him at all. She leaves Elisha to realize on his own that the child has died.

Elisha tells Gehazi to tie up his robe, take the prophet's staff, and run as fast as possible. He orders him not to stop for long greetings on the road, so no time is lost. He instructs Gehazi to lay the staff directly upon the boy's face to help him.

The mother swears by the living Lord and by Elisha's life that she will not go back without the prophet. She had little faith in Gehazi or the staff alone and wanted Elisha there in person. Seeing her intense grief and faith, Elisha gets up and follows her home.

Gehazi runs ahead and lays the staff on the boy's face, but there is no sound or sign of life. He comes back along the road to meet Elisha and reports that the boy has not awakened. This proved that God's power was not a magic trick carried by an object, but comes from the Lord alone.

Elisha arrives at the woman's home and climbs up to his guest room. There he finds the young boy lying dead upon the prophet's own bed, right where the mother had left him. Elisha now faces the reality of the child's death.

Elisha goes inside, shuts the door behind him and the dead child, and prays earnestly to the Lord. Closing the door gave him quiet space to pray without distraction or public show. He knew that only God had the power to bring the dead back to life.

Elisha lies down on the bed and places his mouth, eyes, and hands over the boy's body. Although touching a corpse normally made an Israelite ceremonially unclean, showing mercy and saving a life took priority. As Elisha stretches over the child in prayer, the boy's cold flesh slowly grows warm.

Elisha steps down and paces back and forth across the room in focused prayer before stretching over the child once more. The boy sneezes seven times to clear his head and then opens his eyes. God worked this miracle step by step, showing the power of persevering prayer.

Elisha tells Gehazi to call the Shunammite mother to the room. When she arrives at the doorway, the prophet gently tells her to take up her living boy. Her deep sorrow is suddenly turned into joyful relief.

The woman comes in and falls at Elisha's feet, bowing to the ground in deep reverence and praise to God. She then picks up her living son and walks out of the room. Her quiet trust in the Lord was rewarded with the gift of her child's life restored.

Elisha returns to Gilgal while a severe famine grips the land. A group of student prophets sits before him to learn God's word, and Elisha looks after their physical needs as well. He tells his servant to put a large pot on the fire to boil stew for the whole group.

One of the students goes out into the fields to gather wild plants for the pot. He discovers a wild vine and mistakenly picks a lap full of wild gourds, slicing them into the stew without knowing what they are. These were likely bitter, poisonous gourds that were dangerous to eat.

The stew is served to the hungry prophets, but the first taste is so terribly bitter that they cry out in fear. They shout to Elisha that there is death in the pot, believing the meal is poisoned. In a time of famine, this mistake threatened both their lives and their scarce food supply.

Elisha calls for some flour, throws it into the pot, and tells them to serve the stew to the people. When they eat it, the stew is completely harmless and wholesome. The flour had no natural power to destroy poison, but God used it as a visible sign of His healing power.

A man from Baal-shalishah brings Elisha twenty loaves of fresh barley bread and ripe grain from the first harvest. Under God's law, these first portions belonged to the priests, but faithful believers brought them to God's true prophet during this time of national rebellion. Instead of saving the food for himself during the famine, Elisha tells his servant to feed the people.

The servant questions how twenty small loaves could ever feed a crowd of one hundred men. Elisha repeats the command and gives a promise from the Lord that the men will eat and have food left over. God's promise assured them that the Lord provides far beyond human ability.

The servant places the bread before the men, and they all eat until they are satisfied, leaving leftovers just as the Lord had promised. This miracle foreshadows Jesus feeding large crowds with only a few loaves of bread. It shows that God faithfully cares for His people in times of scarcity.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some older critical scholars argued that the miracle was not a real multiplication of bread, but that the men simply felt satisfied with small portions.
